title: Happy ending for heptagons: ES(7)=33
premise_risks: a special case of a famous conjecture, but the genuine first open case
an intermediate bound between 33 and 113 specific to k=7 might exist (none found)
likely to fall to a large SAT computation; check for a 2026 announcement before publishing
plain: Among any 17 points in the plane with no three on a line, some 6 form a convex hexagon, and 16 points are not enough; this was proved by computer in 2006. Erdős and Szekeres predicted that the right number for convex 7-gons is 33. Prove that every 33 points in general position contain 7 in convex position.
math: Let $ES(k)$ be the least $N$ such that every set of $N$ points in $\mathbb R^2$ with no three collinear contains $k$ points in convex position. Known $ES(k)\ge 2^{k-2}+1$ (Erdős–Szekeres 1961) with equality for $k\le6$; $ES(7)\le 113$. Prove $ES(7)=33$, i.e. every 33-point set in general position contains a convex heptagon (any rigorous improvement of $113$ is also progress).
review_note: Known: $ES(6)=17$: Szekeres & Peters, ANZIAM J. 48 (2006). Small-$k$ bound $ES(k)\le\binom{2k-5}{k-2}-\binom{2k-8}{k-3}+2$ (Mojarrad & Vlachos, DCG 2016, arXiv:1510.06255), giving $ES(7)\le113$; earlier $\binom{2k-5}{k-2}+1=127$ (Tóth–Valtr 2005). Asymptotic $ES(k)\le2^{k+O(\sqrt{k\log k})}$: Suk, JAMS 2017 (refined by Holmsen–Mojarrad–Pach–Tardos). Empty hexagon $h(6)=30$: Heule & Scheucher, arXiv:2403.00737 (SoCG 2024). Dumitru, 'Notes on the 33-point Erdős–Szekeres problem', arXiv:2512.24061 (Dec 2025): SAT encoding, partial UNSAT only.
